source.title: Nonlinear Schrödinger equation on graphs: recent results and open problems

accepted.question_text: Let a graph be obtained as a limit of a network of thin tubes or guides joined at junctions, and let a nonlinear Schrödinger equation be posed on the shrinking tube system before the limit is taken. Does the vanishing-transverse-size limit produce a nonlinear Schrödinger equation on the limiting graph, and if so, which vertex boundary conditions appear at the junction? More specifically, how do the limiting vertex conditions depend on the way the tubes and junction are shrunk and on the boundary conditions imposed on the tube walls, such as Neumann or Dirichlet conditions?

evidence.quote: The graph should be a limit in some sense of a more realistic systems of thin tubes (or guides) connecting at junctions. A first problem is getting the limit of a certain dynamical model, e.g. NLS equation defined on the system of thin guides when transversal size of tube vanishes. It is reasonable to conjecture that this limit should be a NLS on a graph as defined before, but with which boundary conditions? And how the boundary conditions at the vertex could depend on the limit process of shrinking the tubes, guides and junction size? A further difficulty could be the dependence of limit process on the conditions at the boundary of the thin tube, e.g. Neumann or Dirichlet.

These problems have been tackled, with partial solution, in the linear case (see [29, 30, 31] and reference therein). They remain open for nonlinear models, where there is no literature, with the only exception (to the knowledge of the present author) of a series of papers about the reduction of the Ginzburg-Landau equation and its stationary counterpart from thin tubes to graphs

accepted.question_text: Can one derive an effective one-dimensional Gross–Pitaevskii or nonlinear Schrödinger dynamics on graph-like structures, such as a Y-junction, directly from a many-body Bose system or another first-principles model? In particular, if one starts from an N-body theory on a graph and takes the many-particle limit with suitable scalings, how should the vertex or defect boundary conditions be handled in the limiting equation, given that even the corresponding problem for a line with a single defect is still open?

evidence.quote: A second point of view is less phenomenological, and related to the deduction of evolution equation for Bose Einstein condensates from first principle.

Being confident that a Gross-Pitaevskii equation realizes the correct quasi one dimensional limit, a similar procedure could be attempted on graphlike structure, for example on a Y-junction; to simplify the analysis, one could start directly from a N-body theory on the graph, and to attempt at taking the N→∞ limit with suitable scalings. Notice that the main problem, i.e. the treatment of the boundary condition, it is open also in the simplest case of a graph with two edges, i.e. a line with a defect.

accepted.question_text: Is the nonlinear Schrödinger equation on trees well posed? More precisely, for a tree graph equipped with the relevant vertex coupling conditions, can one prove existence, uniqueness, and appropriate continuous dependence for solutions in the natural energy spaces, analogous to the well-posedness theory available for the star-graph case?

evidence.quote: in [24] a generalization of this systems to trees (including star graphs) is studied as a model of cardiovascular system, and in particular it is shown that BBM on a tree is well posed. It is interesting that (see [25]) travelling waves for BBM equation on a tree have been recently constructed for particular vertex conditions. By the way a result of well posedness of NLS on trees in not yet proven, although well plausible; a step in this direction with proof of relevant dispersive estimates is given in [26, 27].

accepted.question_text: When the threshold condition ensuring existence of an absolute constrained minimizer fails for the action functional on a star graph, does the action still possess a local constrained minimum that is strictly larger than its infimum? Likewise, when the analogous threshold fails for the energy constrained at fixed mass, does the constrained energy still have a local constrained minimum above its infimum?

evidence.quote: The bad behaviour of the Kirchhoff junction ( α = 0) prevents the action with α small, or the energy with a big m, to have a constrained absolute minimum. It is a conjecture that the action has a local constrained minimum that is larger than the infimum when the condition −N√ω < α < α∗ fails, and similarly for the constrained energy with a corresponding condition on mass.

accepted.question_text: Can the orbital-stability and instability analysis for standing waves of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation be extended from star graphs to more complex graphs, such as trees or graphs with loops? In such settings, where explicit formulas for stationary states are generally unavailable, can one still identify standing-wave branches and verify the spectral and variational conditions needed to prove stability or instability?

evidence.quote: One could ask if a similar analysis could be performed on more complex graphs, for example trees or graphs with loops. Of course the fact that stationary states on star graphs are completely known, which is a rare case, is a strong facilitation in obtaining precise results. In the case of less trivial graphs it is generally impossible to obtain explicitly standing waves, but some simple non trivial graphs can be probably treated along the lines discussed.

accepted.question_text: For nonlinear Schrödinger equations on graphs whose linear part has eigenvalues, bifurcation theory can produce nonlinear standing-wave branches that emerge from linear bound states. How can one also obtain and analyze branches of nonlinear standing waves that have no linear counterpart, such as nonlinear excited or bound states that do not bifurcate from the zero solution?

evidence.quote: A second problem is that bifurcation theory allows to identify branches of nonlinear stationary states which have a linear counterpart, but how to obtain branches of states without linear counterpart, which exist as we know from the example of nonlinear excited states in star graphs? A guess is that excited or in general bound states without linear counterpart bifurcate from (not small) solitary waves turning on the external potential.

accepted.question_text: What new nonlinear Schrödinger dynamics arise on graphs when one changes the vertex boundary conditions away from the standard cases studied here? In particular, can different vertex couplings produce new branches of standing waves, bifurcations of ground states, or symmetry-breaking phenomena analogous to those known for the line with a δ′ interaction?

evidence.quote: A different extension could be in the direction of different boundary conditions at the vertices. In such a case one expects new dynamical effects, for example bifurcation and symmetry breaking of ground states as proved for the NLS on the line with δ′ interaction (see[49]).

accepted.question_text: Are standing waves of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation on graphs asymptotically stable? More precisely, if a solution starts close in the energy norm to a standing wave e^{iωt}Φ_ω, does the solution converge at large time to another nearby standing wave plus a dispersive linear term and a decaying remainder? In order to prove such a result, can one develop the necessary analysis of the Hamiltonian linearization JL on graphs, including spectral information and dispersive estimates for exp(tJL), and can this be done for important cases such as subcritical power nonlinearities, where the methods described in the paper presently fail?

evidence.quote: A final open and difficult problem is the so called asymptotic stability of standing waves. In our case a standing wave Φωeiωt is said asymptotically stable if for every solution u(t) starting near Φω in the energy norm, one has the representation u(t) = eiω∞tΦω∞ + Ut∗ Ψ∞ + R∞(t)

Part of the difficulties are due to the fact that the Hamiltonian structure plays a role in the analysis and this makes unavoidable to study the spectrum of the not selfadjoint and not skew adjoint operator JL (the Hamiltonian linearization) and to get dispersive estimates about its evolution exp( tJL ); this introduces some interesting and new mathematical problems about operators on graphs, already at the linear level. Moreover the proof of possible asymptotic stability requires a control of the decay of nonlinear remainders; this control depends in a critical way on several analytical tools (in particular dispersive Strichartz estimates) which at present work only for restricted classes of nonlinearities; for example, for subcritical power nonlinearities the procedure fails.

accepted.question_text: Do multisoliton states exist for the nonlinear Schrödinger equation on star graphs, and what happens when several solitons collide simultaneously at a vertex? In particular, can one construct or analyze solutions representing more than one incoming or outgoing soliton interacting through the junction?

evidence.quote: Nothing it is presently known about the possible existence of multisolitons, or about the collision of several solitons at the vertex.

accepted.question_text: How do solitons scatter on graphs with nontrivial topology beyond the simple star-graph setting? In particular, for graphs such as trees or other networks with internal structure, can one rigorously describe propagation and scattering of solitons and determine how the topology and available dispersive estimates affect the dynamics?

evidence.quote: On the contrary, scattering of solitons on graphs having a less trivial topology is an open problem. In particular it could be interesting the study of propagation of solitons on trees, about which something has been said before in relation to BBM equation. Notice that among the main technical ingredients are Strichartz estimates, and every generalization needs their validity.

accepted.question_text: Can one extend the time interval over which the post-collision dynamics of a fast soliton on a graph is accurately approximated by outgoing solitary waves? More specifically, beyond the logarithmic-in-velocity timescale obtained in the paper, are there longer timescales of validity, perhaps depending on the initial data or on the vertex interaction, for which the outgoing-wave approximation remains accurate?

evidence.quote: Another important problem concerns the possibility of extending the timescale of validity of approximation by the solitary outgoing waves. In a different model (scattering of two solitons on the line) in [54], some considerations are given about the possibility of longer timescales of outgoing soliton approximation depending on the initial data and external potential, but it is unclear whether similar considerations can be applied to the present case.

accepted.question_text: For nonlinear Schrödinger equations on graphs with nonlinearities that are close to, but not exactly, the integrable cubic case, do outgoing waves produced by a fast soliton-vertex interaction remain close to solitons on timescales comparable to those proved for cubic NLS? In other words, how stable is the fast-soliton scattering picture under non-integrable perturbations of the cubic nonlinearity?

evidence.quote: As regards the limitation to cubic NLS, the fundamental asymptotics proved in [52] and used to get the analogous result on graphs depend on the integrability of cubic NLS. One can conjecture that for nonlinearities close to integrable the outgoing waves are close to solitons over timescale similar to the above ones.

accepted.question_text: Can one develop a rigorous mathematical theory for the capture and generation of solitons in nonlinear Schrödinger dynamics on graphs? More specifically, in dynamical regimes that lie between the standing-wave regime and the fast-soliton-scattering regime, can one explain when junction interactions or graph geometry trap a soliton, create a new one, or transfer mass into a localized coherent structure?

evidence.quote: Many interesting physical phenomena experimentally well tested are probably in a different or intermediate region. In particular capture and generation of solitons are not yet understood from a rigorous point of view, and they represent a challenge to mathematical methods and theoretical interpretation where perhaps the simple but non trivial model of NLS equation on graphs could offer some insight.
